description: Un grupo de amigos apasionados por el código, el aprendizaje y resolver problemas sin complicarnos la vida. Venimos a pasarla bien, aprender cosas nuevas en el camino y construir una solución de la que nos sintamos orgullosos.
summary:
Ka’anluum (“sky” and “land” in Maya) is an offline mobile app that helps milpa farmers in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula decide what to plant over the next two years, so their soil can recover while protecting their harvest. In some areas, milpa fallow periods have fallen from more than 20 years to around seven, putting greater pressure on the soil.

Farmers answer four simple questions. The app assesses their land—new, healthy, showing signs of fatigue, or tired—and compares three two-year strategies: planting maize every year, growing maize with jack bean between the rows, or planting one jack bean cover cycle followed by maize.

Using 28 years of NASA POWER rainfall and temperature data (GPM IMERG and MERRA-2) for the plot’s coordinates, the app shows how many months the soil remains bare and how sowing dates compare in terms of dry-spell exposure during maize flowering.

The app speaks, uses words in Maya and Spanish, requires no account, and never promises yields. It offers options; the farmer makes the decision. The information was already out there. We’re building a bridge to the people who grow our food.
details:
What it does. Ka'anluum turns NASA Earth observation data into a two-year planting plan that a milpa farmer can understand without reading charts. It answers one question: how do I plant my plot for the next two years without wearing out my land?

How it works.

1. Four questions.

- Where the plot is: on the map, by GPS or by choosing the municipality.

- How the land has been used: how many years in a row it has been planted, whether it rests, whether it is burned, how the last harvest went, whether it shows signs of tiredness, or whether it is forest that has never been planted.

- What soil it has and how big it is.

- What the farmer needs most: food, income or caring for the land.

2. Diagnosis of the land. A transparent rule classifies the land as new, healthy, getting tired or tired, and shows the reasons on screen. It also shows how many of the next 24 months the soil would sit bare if nothing changes.

3. Three 2-year strategies. The app always shows all three:

- maize every year, the current practice;

- maize with jack bean (Canavalia ensiformis) between the rows;

- one jack bean cover cycle followed by maize.

The diagnosis and the farmer's priority decide which one is suggested. Each card states why it is suggested, what the data says, what the soil gains, what we don't know yet and what to check with a technician.

4. Best sowing date. The app uses 28 years of NASA POWER rainfall and heat data at the plot's coordinates. For each date in the official sowing window, it counts in how many years a dry spell of 5 or more days hit maize flowering. In Tekax, sowing on June 1 gives 20 of 28 years, and sowing on July 15 gives all 28. That means 13% versus 51% of flowering days in drought.

Example. Don José has planted maize on the same plot for 4 years or more, never lets it rest and burns before sowing. His land comes out as "tired", and it would sit bare 14 of the next 24 months. Because he needs to keep eating from his milpa, the app suggests maize with jack bean between the rows: two more months with a crop in the field and a nitrogen-fixing legume, without losing his harvest. Juan is about to clear forest for the first time. The app suggests starting with a cover crop from year one, without burning and leaving strips of forest standing.

Benefits.

- Farmers see when their soil is exposed and how to cover it.

- They choose a sowing date backed by 28 years of data from their own area.

- Every number shows its source, its period, how many years were evaluated and what is still unconfirmed.

- The final decision stays with the farmer and their technician. The app suggests; it never promises yields.

Expected impact.

- Close the gap between climate data that already exists and the rainfed farmers who plant.

- Help the milpa keep producing with short fallow periods, without clearing more forest.

- Next steps: field-test with milpa farmers and INIFAP technicians in Tekax, add SMAP soil moisture and the stages of beans and squash, and grow from one municipality to the whole peninsula.

Tools.

- App: Progressive Web App in vanilla JavaScript (ES modules and Vite), IndexedDB and a service worker to work offline, the Web Speech API to read options aloud and take voice commands, and Leaflet for the map.

- Server: Python with FastAPI, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, SQLAlchemy and Alembic, running in Docker. Deployed on Render with the database on Supabase.

- Data: a Python pipeline that downloads NASA POWER data, and a script that audits the published data against a fresh download.

- Tests: 56 automated tests in the app, and 27 in the server plus 3 integration tests against PostgreSQL.

- Hardware: nothing special. A phone with a web browser is enough.

- AI support: declared in the Use of Artificial Intelligence field.

Why it is creative.

- It answers a farmer's question, not a technician's: instead of rainfall maps, it says "how many months your land stays bare" and "which day is best for you to sow".

- It uses hand-held signs, Maya and Spanish words and a 24-month strip instead of charts.

- It crosses climate events with the plant stage that suffers most: knowing there was a drought is not enough, the question is whether it hit flowering.

- It always shows all three options, including the one the farmer already uses, so they compare instead of being told what to do.

What the team took into account.

- No signal in the field: the app works offline after it is opened once.

- Reading and language: it reads options aloud, takes voice commands and uses Maya and Spanish names.

- Privacy: no account is needed, the exact location stays on the phone, and the server only receives aggregated data with consent.

- Honesty with the data:

- It shows historical exposure, not a forecast, and the app says so.

- An incomplete year is never counted as a year without drought.

- When evidence is missing, the app shows "No estimate" instead of zero risk.
